description: We are high school students working to solve this  challenge
summary: We built Clavius to explore a question a lunar mission team could face after a launch delay: if touchdown moves by a week, how will sunlight and Earth visibility change? The application uses NASA terrain data and ephemerides to compare landing dates at Connecting Ridge and Shackleton rim near the Moon's south pole. In one saved Shackleton comparison, moving touchdown from January 8 to January 15, 2028, reduced first-day Earth visibility from 24 hours to zero, while the Sun remained visible throughout the later day. Users can inspect the horizon to understand the difference, then carry their selected site and time into a flight rehearsal and simulated rover traverse. Clavius addresses the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge by making these trade-offs easier to examine. We want mission teams to explore alternatives when schedules change, and students to understand why a sunlit lunar location can still present power and communication problems.
details:
Compare landing sites and dates

A Clavius session starts with a landing date and the constraints the user cares about. Someone planning a solar-powered rover might prioritize energy. A team expecting to send science data home might limit how long Earth can stay out of view.

Clavius compares three dates at each of two sites and evaluates three Earth-to-Moon transfer durations for every option. Users can apply limits on sunlight, Earth outages, local slope and transfer budget, then move through the hours after touchdown. The horizon plot shows the Sun and Earth above the surrounding terrain, with visibility bands and estimates of the next rise or set.

This gives planners a common comparison to discuss and educators an interactive example of lunar conditions.

Calculate local conditions using NASA data

We focused on two sites so we could account for local terrain and more distant ridges:

  • PGDA78: NASA LOLA elevations at 5-meter posting near each site.
  • PGDA90: An 80-meter regional elevation grid for the surrounding terrain.
  • JPL SPICE: Sun and Earth directions at the selected time.
  • LROC imagery: Surface images and stereo relief for visual route planning.

Solar calculations account for terrain obstruction, the visible fraction of the Sun and panel orientation. That distinction mattered in the January 15, 2028, Shackleton scenario: despite sunlight throughout the day, a level panel received about 65 watt-hours per square meter, compared with 146 a week earlier.

We considered uncertainty in the terrain, observer height and sampling intervals because each can affect the calculated horizon or visibility windows.

Follow the selected mission

The selected landing site and touchdown time carry through to the flight and rover views. Users inspect a simplified flight rehearsal, place waypoints on LROC imagery and assign our hypothetical Clavius R1 rover a science or parking task.

MuJoCo simulates the drive on the nominal LOLA terrain. Replay and mission analysis show the traveled path, reached waypoints, attitude and battery changes beside the original landing conditions.

Our creative choice was to connect the comparison to a scenario users can follow and inspect, with the same site and time linking each stage. The flight includes a prescribed descent, and the rover uses declared friction and power properties.

Tools used

We built the browser interface with JavaScript and TypeScript, using React, Three.js and Recharts. The backend uses Python and FastAPI, with NumPy and SciPy for numerical calculations. JPL SPICE supplies astronomical geometry, and MuJoCo runs the main rover traverse simulation.

Validation and intended impact

We checked 32 calculated Sun and Earth directions against JPL Horizons and compared modeled shadows with lunar camera observations. The direction checks passed their thresholds, while several shadow-comparison and numerical-refinement targets remain unmet.

Five-meter terrain posting leaves wheel-scale obstacles unresolved. Earth visibility establishes a geometric opportunity for direct communication; antenna performance, radio link margin and ground-station availability require further analysis.

These limits shape the project's intended use as an early planning and educational prototype. We want teams to explore alternatives when schedules change and students to understand how terrain and timing affect lunar missions. Saved results retain source hashes and model assumptions so users can revisit a decision and examine what produced it.
